articles.title: Does Numbing Cream Affect a Tattoo?
articles.mt: Does Numbing Cream Affect a Tattoo? | Senseless
articles.md: Does numbing cream affect a tattoo, the ink, or how it settles? What artists actually raise, what nobody can honestly claim, and how to decide with yours.
articles.summary: The question artists ask more often than clients do — what is actually known, what isn't, and why your artist's answer outranks ours.
articles.body:
This is the question a tattoo artist asks, and it is a fairer question than the one clients usually ask. A client wants to know whether preparation is allowed. An artist wants to know whether it changes the skin they are about to work on, the way the ink sits, or how the piece looks in six months.

The short answer: nobody selling numbing cream is in a position to tell you it has no effect on your tattoo, and you should be wary of any brand that does. What we can tell you is what artists actually raise, what is genuinely unknown, and why the person holding the machine is the one whose answer counts.

Why we won't give you a straight yes or no

Senseless is a cosmetic product. We are not permitted to make claims about how a preparation performs on skin during a procedure, and we would not be able to substantiate one here even if we were. There is no body of published work on cosmetic topical preparations and tattoo outcomes that would let anyone answer this honestly in a sentence.

What you will find instead, on plenty of other sites, is a confident no. Treat that as a marketing position rather than a finding. A brand that cannot show you its evidence is telling you what it wants to be true.

What artists actually raise

Concerns cluster around the condition of the skin on the day rather than around the ink itself. The ones that come up most often:

  • Texture and firmness — some artists say prepared skin can feel different to work on, and that they are working by feel as much as by sight.
  • Swelling — a common concern, and one artists raise about a long sitting generally, not only about preparation.
  • Residue — anything left on the surface has to come off before the stencil goes on, which is a workflow point rather than a skin one.
  • Consistency — an artist who has built a method over years has calibrated it against skin they know. Introducing a variable on the day is the objection, and it is a reasonable one.

What is actually knowable

A few things are simply matters of fact rather than opinion:

  • Preparation is applied before the appointment, to clean and unbroken skin. It is not applied to a tattoo in progress or to broken skin.
  • Your artist cleans and prepares the area before the stencil and before any work starts. Nothing you applied at home is still sitting on the surface when the needle goes in.
  • Senseless is a cosmetic product, formulated in the United Kingdom and assessed under a Cosmetic Product Safety Report. It is not a medicine and needs no prescription.
  • What it is not is a decision that belongs to us. It belongs to your artist.

The difference between "allowed" and "advisable"

Plenty of artists are relaxed about it. Plenty are not. A few will end a booking over it, and they are entitled to — it is their work, their reputation, and their name on the piece. None of that is a comment on the product; it is a comment on how that artist likes to work.

The mistake clients make is treating this as a rule to be looked up. It is not a rule. It is a working relationship, and the only way to get the answer is to ask the person you booked with.

How to have the conversation

Ask when you book, not on the day. An artist told a fortnight in advance can plan around it. An artist told on arrival has a client in the chair, a stencil to place, and a schedule behind them.

Say what you are considering, ask whether they would rather you didn't, and take the answer at face value. If they say no, that is the end of it. If they say yes, ask whether they want it applied at a particular time or removed at a particular point — some have a preference, and following it is the whole point of asking.

If your artist says no

Then you go without, and that is a completely normal way to get tattooed. Eat properly beforehand, sleep, skip alcohol, book a length of sitting you can actually sit through, and tell your artist when you need a break. Those are the things every experienced client already does, and they cost nothing.

See the range for tattoo appointments →

articles.title: Can You Use Numbing Cream Before a Tattoo?
articles.mt: Can You Use Numbing Cream Before a Tattoo? | Senseless
articles.md: Can you use numbing cream before a tattoo in the UK? What's legal, what studios allow, what to ask your artist, and how to prepare properly.
articles.summary: Legal, common, and entirely your artist's call — the three-part answer, and the order to deal with them in.
articles.body:
Usually asked as one question, this is really three: is it legal, will the studio allow it, and is it sensible for the piece you have booked. They have different answers and they need dealing with in that order.

The short answer: yes, you can buy and use a cosmetic topical preparation in the UK without a prescription — but whether you should use it before your appointment is your artist's decision, not a legal one, and asking them is the step people skip.

The legal part

Cosmetic topical preparations are sold openly in the UK and need no prescription. Senseless is a cosmetic product, formulated in the United Kingdom by Matrix Health Group Ltd and assessed under a Cosmetic Product Safety Report before it is sold. Buying one is not a grey area.

Prescription products are a different category with a different route, and if a pharmacist or a doctor is the right source for you, that is where to go. This page is about the cosmetic category.

The studio part, which is the one that matters

Studios set their own policies and artists have their own preferences within them. Some are entirely relaxed. Some ask clients not to. A few will not tattoo someone who has applied anything, and will say so on their booking form.

None of this is inconsistency — it is a room full of professionals with different methods. The practical consequence is simple: the studio's answer overrides everything on this page, and you find it out by asking rather than by reading.

Ask at the right moment

When you book, not on the day. A message at booking gives your artist a fortnight to say "fine, but apply it at this point" or "I'd rather you didn't". Raising it while you are sitting down with the stencil ready is how a good appointment starts badly.

What to say is short: that you are thinking about using a topical preparation beforehand, and would they rather you did or didn't. That is the whole message.

If the answer is yes

Then the questions become practical ones, and most of them are about the booking rather than the product:

  • How long are you sitting? The length of the appointment is what the three Senseless strengths are matched to — Clinical for shorter sessions, Advanced for longer or more sensitive ones, Professional for the longest and most demanding.
  • How big is the area? That decides format rather than strength. Cream is general-purpose, gel is precise on smaller defined areas, spray suits broad areas like a limb or a back piece.
  • Have you patch tested? Twenty-four hours beforehand, on the inside of the wrist or behind the ear. Don't use it if you see any reaction.
  • Does your artist want it applied at a particular time? If they have a preference, follow it. Their window takes precedence over any general guidance.

What it is applied to

Clean, unbroken skin, ahead of the appointment. Not broken skin, not skin that is healing, not a tattoo in progress. Apply a visible layer that sits on the surface rather than rubbing it in, and follow the directions on the product and your artist's instruction.

If the answer is no

Take it at face value and prepare the way experienced clients do anyway. Sleep. Eat a proper meal beforehand rather than arriving on an empty stomach. Skip alcohol the night before. Book a sitting you can actually sit through rather than the longest one available, and tell your artist when you need a break — every good artist would rather stop for five minutes than have a client tense up for an hour.

articles.title: Do Tattoo Artists Use Numbing Cream?
articles.mt: Do Tattoo Artists Use Numbing Cream? | Senseless
articles.md: Do tattoo artists use numbing cream on clients? Why studio policies differ so much, what changed, and how to ask yours without getting it wrong.
articles.summary: Some do, some won't, and the split is more interesting than either camp admits.
articles.body:
Ask five artists and you will get a range of answers, delivered with more conviction than the question probably deserves. It is worth understanding why the profession is split, because it tells you how to ask your own artist.

The short answer: some artists offer it, some allow clients to bring their own, and some refuse outright. The split is genuine and long-standing, and no artist is being unreasonable at either end of it.

The case artists make against it

Artists who say no tend to give versions of the same four reasons:

  • Method. An artist works partly by feel, on skin they have learned to read over years. Anything that changes the surface on the day is a variable in a process they have calibrated.
  • Responsibility. If the client supplied the product, the artist has no idea what is on the skin they are working on. Some are simply not willing to work under that condition.
  • The sitting. A blunter version: discomfort is information. A client who cannot sit through a session may be booking too long a session, and some artists would rather that conversation happened than be papered over.
  • Ritual. A minority hold that the experience is part of it. You do not have to agree, but it is an honest position honestly held.

The case artists make for it

Artists who are relaxed about it are usually making a practical argument rather than a philosophical one. A client who sits still is easier to work on than one who flinches. Long sittings finish in one appointment rather than two. Nervous first-timers come back. And some studios simply see it as a normal client comfort measure, no more remarkable than a cushion or a fan.

Why studio policy varies so much

There is no single governing body setting one rule for UK tattooing on this. Studios are licensed by their local authority for hygiene and premises, and the day-to-day working method inside them is the artist's own. That is why two studios on the same street can hold opposite policies without either being wrong.

It also means a policy you read about online — or an artist's opinion on social media — tells you about that artist, not about yours.

Artists who supply their own

Some studios apply a preparation themselves as part of the appointment. If yours does, that settles it: use theirs, on their timing, and don't bring anything. Turning up having already applied something to a studio that provides its own is the version of this that causes the most friction, because it puts the artist in the position of not knowing what is on the skin.

How to ask yours

Directly, at booking, and without arguing the point. "Are you happy for me to use a topical preparation beforehand, or would you rather I didn't?" is the entire message. You will get a clear answer, and the answer is final.

What not to do is ask on the day, apply it without mentioning it, or quote another artist's policy at yours. All three convert a small logistical question into a bad start.

What we sell, and what we don't claim about it

Senseless is a cosmetic topical preparation, formulated in the United Kingdom and assessed under a Cosmetic Product Safety Report, in three strengths across cream, gel and spray. We match the range to the length of the sitting and the size of the area. What we don't do is tell you your artist should say yes — that is not a decision a brand gets to make.

articles.title: What to Tell Your Artist About Numbing Cream
articles.mt: What to Tell Your Artist About Numbing Cream
articles.md: Exactly what to say to your tattoo artist about numbing cream, when to say it, and what to do with the answer. A short script you can copy.
articles.summary: A message you can send at booking, the four details worth including, and what to do with each possible answer.
articles.body:
Most of the friction around this comes down to timing and phrasing rather than the product. An artist told at booking has options. An artist told in the chair has a problem. Here is the conversation, in the order it works best.

The short answer: message your artist when you book, say what you are considering in one line, ask whether they would rather you did or didn't, and follow the answer exactly — including any instruction about timing.

When to raise it

At booking. Not the night before, and not on arrival. Your artist is planning a session and a schedule; a fortnight's notice lets them fold your question into that, or tell you no while you still have time to think about it.

What to say

Short and neutral works better than a paragraph of justification:

"Before the appointment — are you happy for me to use a topical numbing preparation beforehand, or would you rather I didn't? Happy either way, just want to check."

That gives them a clear question, a clear out, and no sense that they are being talked into something.

The four details worth adding if they say yes

  • What it is. A cosmetic topical preparation, not a prescription product. Name the brand and the strength if they ask — most won't, but the ones who do will want to know.
  • When you plan to apply it. Ask if they want it at a particular point. If they give you a window, theirs replaces any general guidance.
  • Where. Confirm the area with them, particularly if the piece wraps or the placement is not yet final.
  • That you've patch tested. Twenty-four hours beforehand. It answers the question they would otherwise have to ask.

What to do with each answer

  • "Yes, that's fine." Follow their timing if they gave you one, and apply to clean, unbroken skin ahead of the appointment.
  • "I'd rather you didn't." Then don't, and don't negotiate. It is their work.
  • "We use our own." Use theirs. Don't bring anything and don't apply anything beforehand.
  • "Up to you." Take the decision yourself, and still tell them on the day that you did — so nothing about the skin surprises them.

On the day

Tell them again, briefly, when you arrive: that you applied it, when, and where. Ten seconds. It is the single thing that keeps this from becoming an issue, and artists notice clients who do it.

What not to do

  • Don't apply anything without telling them. This is the one that damages the relationship.
  • Don't spring it on them in the chair.
  • Don't quote another artist's or another studio's policy at them.
  • Don't apply more than the directions say because you think it will do more. Follow the product guidance.
  • Don't apply it to broken or healing skin. It goes on clean, unbroken skin only.

articles.title: Where to Buy Numbing Cream for Tattoos in the UK
articles.mt: Where to Buy Numbing Cream for Tattoos in the UK
articles.md: Where to buy numbing cream for tattoos in the UK, what to check before you order, and the difference between a cosmetic product and a pharmacy medicine.
articles.summary: The four places people buy from, what to check on any of them, and why the label matters more than the price.
articles.body:
Searching this in the UK turns up marketplace listings, a pharmacy category, a handful of specialist brands and a lot of imported packaging. They are not the same kind of thing, and the differences are worth ten minutes before you order.

The short answer: you can buy a cosmetic topical preparation in the UK without a prescription, from a specialist brand, a marketplace or a studio. What separates them is whether the seller can tell you who assessed the product, what is in it, and which UK company stands behind it.

The four routes, and what each one gets you

  • A UK specialist brand. Sells one category and knows it. You should be able to find the company, the ingredients and the safety assessment without hunting. The Senseless range is here.
  • A marketplace listing. Fast and often cheap. The seller may be a reseller several steps from whoever made it, and the listing may not tell you which.
  • A pharmacy. A different regulatory category — pharmacy products are medicines, with their own documentation and their own route. If that is what you need, a pharmacist is the right person to ask.
  • Your studio. Some sell or supply their own. If yours does, that is the simplest answer available and it removes the conversation entirely.

What to check before you order

Five things, and all five should take under a minute to find on a page that has nothing to hide:

  • A named UK company. Not just a brand name — a registered company you can look up. Senseless is Matrix Health Group Ltd, VAT GB 523 781 682.
  • A full ingredients list. Cosmetic products carry an INCI list. If you can't see one, that is information in itself.
  • A safety assessment. UK cosmetic products are assessed under a Cosmetic Product Safety Report before sale. Ask whether the product has one.
  • The size, stated plainly. Price means nothing without it. Compare per gram or per millilitre, not per tube. Ours are cream in 10g and 30g, gel in 15ml and 35ml, and spray in 35ml.
  • Where it ships from. An import can sit in customs past your appointment date, and returning it is a different proposition.

Cosmetic product or medicine — the distinction that matters

These are two regulatory categories, not two quality levels. A cosmetic topical preparation is sold openly and needs no prescription. A medicine has its own classification, its own documentation and its own supply route, and a pharmacist or prescriber is the right source.

Senseless is a cosmetic product. That is a statement about which category it sits in, not a claim that it is better or worse than something in the other one. If a practitioner has told you that you need a medical preparation, follow that.

Buying for an appointment date

Order with a working day in hand. Standard UK delivery is free on orders over £40 and next-day is free over £80; ordering before 1pm on a working day means the parcel is dispatched the same day. A weekend or a bank holiday moves dispatch to the next working day, which is the thing that catches people out.

Patch test 24 hours before you plan to use it — which means the parcel needs to arrive with more than a day to spare, not the morning of.

Before you buy anything at all

Ask your artist. A studio that prefers you didn't, or that supplies its own, makes the whole question moot — and finding that out after the parcel arrives is a waste of both the money and the delivery slot.

articles.title: Tattoo Aftercare: The First 48 Hours
articles.mt: Tattoo Aftercare: The First 48 Hours | Senseless
articles.md: What to do in the first 48 hours after a tattoo — wrapping, the first wash, what to avoid, and when to ask for help. Your studio's instructions come first.
articles.summary: The two days that set up everything after them — and why your artist's instructions outrank every guide online, including this one.
articles.body:
The first two days are the ones people get wrong, usually by doing too much rather than too little. Here is what generally happens, in order — with one instruction that comes before all of it.

The short answer: follow the aftercare instructions your artist gave you. They know the piece, the placement, the wrap they used and how they work. Where this guide and your studio disagree, your studio wins.

Why your artist's instructions come first

Aftercare advice varies between studios because the wrapping does. An artist using an adhesive second-skin film gives different instructions from one using cling film, and both differ again from a dry dressing. A guide that tells you to remove your wrap after two hours is useless to someone whose artist applied a film meant to stay on for days.

So: read what they gave you. If you have lost it, message the studio. They would far rather answer a question than see the result of a guess.

Hours 0 to 24 — the wrap

Your artist will have told you which of two situations you are in:

  • A traditional wrap — usually removed after a few hours, on their timing, then the first wash.
  • An adhesive second-skin film — usually left in place considerably longer, often several days. Fluid collecting under it is normal and does not mean something is wrong.

Whichever you have, wash your hands before you touch anything near it. That single habit matters more than any product in the routine.

The first wash

Once your artist's window has passed, the general routine is:

  • Clean hands first, every time.
  • Lukewarm water — not hot.
  • A gentle, fragrance-free cleanser, worked with fingertips rather than a cloth, flannel or sponge.
  • Rinse thoroughly so nothing is left on the skin.
  • Pat dry with a clean paper towel rather than a bath towel, and let it air for a few minutes.
  • A thin layer of whatever your artist recommended. Thin is the operative word — a thick layer traps moisture against the skin.

The Senseless Foaming Cleanser is an antibacterial cleanser, suitable for use before treatment and on freshly treated skin, and the Vitamin A & D Ointment is a simple barrier ointment for keeping freshly treated skin comfortable and protected. If your artist named a specific product, use theirs.

Hours 24 to 48

Repeat the wash routine, usually twice a day. Expect the area to feel warm, look a little red at the edges, and weep a small amount of plasma and ink — that is ordinary in the first couple of days. Tightness as it dries is also ordinary.

What to avoid

  • Soaking. No baths, swimming pools, sea or hot tubs. Showers are fine; sitting in water is not.
  • Sun. Keep it covered and out of direct sunlight. Sunscreen goes on later, once the skin has settled — not on fresh work.
  • Picking and scratching. The itch arrives; nothing good comes of answering it.
  • Tight clothing over the area, and anything abrasive.
  • The gym. Sweat, shared equipment and friction — give it a few days and ask your artist about your specific placement.
  • Re-wrapping unless your artist told you to.

When to contact someone

Contact your artist if you are unsure about anything — that is what they are there for, and no reputable studio minds. Seek medical advice if you develop spreading redness, increasing pain after the first couple of days rather than decreasing, significant swelling, discharge that is not clear plasma, a fever, or a red streak spreading from the area. That is a matter for a pharmacist, a GP or NHS 111 rather than for a website, and it is not something to wait out.

What comes next

Tattoo healing stages, day by day →

Tattoo aftercare products →

faq.question: How long do I leave the wrap on after a tattoo?
faq.answer: Whatever your artist told you, because it depends on what they used. A traditional wrap usually comes off after a few hours; an adhesive second-skin film often stays on considerably longer. If you have lost the instructions, message the studio rather than guessing.

faq.question: How do I do the first wash?
faq.answer: Clean hands, lukewarm water, a gentle fragrance-free cleanser worked with fingertips rather than a cloth, rinse thoroughly, pat dry with a clean paper towel, then a thin layer of whatever your artist recommended.

faq.question: Is it normal for a new tattoo to weep?
faq.answer: A small amount of plasma and ink in the first couple of days is ordinary, as is warmth, tightness and a little redness at the edges. Spreading redness, increasing pain after the first days, significant swelling, discharge that is not clear plasma, or a fever are reasons to seek medical advice.

faq.question: Can I shower with a new tattoo?
faq.answer: Showering is generally fine; soaking is not. No baths, swimming pools, sea or hot tubs until your artist says otherwise.

faq.question: When can I go back to the gym?
faq.answer: Sweat, shared equipment and friction all argue for waiting a few days, and the right answer depends on your placement. Ask your artist about yours.

faq.question: What should I put on it?
faq.answer: What your artist recommended, in a thin layer. If they left it open to you, a fragrance-free cleanser and a simple barrier ointment are the two products the routine actually needs.

articles.title: Tattoo Healing Stages, Day by Day
articles.mt: Tattoo Healing Stages, Day by Day | Senseless
articles.md: The stages a new tattoo goes through, roughly week by week — what's ordinary at each point, what isn't, and when to ask your artist or a doctor.
articles.summary: Four stages, roughly when each one arrives, and what is ordinary at each — with the caveat that everyone's timeline is their own.
articles.body:
Knowing roughly what comes next removes most of the worry, because almost everything that alarms people in the second week is the ordinary middle of the process. A caveat before the timeline: these are rough stages, not a schedule. Placement, size, your skin and your artist's method all move the dates, and your own timeline is not wrong for differing from a list on a website.

The short answer: broadly four stages — the raw days, the flaking, the dull or cloudy phase, and settling — spread over several weeks on the surface and longer underneath. Your artist's aftercare instructions govern throughout.

Stage one — the first few days

The area is warm, tender, a little red at the edges, and may weep a small amount of plasma and ink. It feels tight as it dries. This is the stage covered by your artist's wrapping instructions and the first-wash routine, and it is the one where clean hands matter most.

What is ordinary: warmth, tenderness, tightness, a small amount of clear or ink-tinted fluid. What is not: spreading redness, pain that increases after the first couple of days rather than easing, significant swelling, discharge that is not clear plasma, or a fever.

Stage two — flaking and itching

Usually arriving within the first week or two, this is the stage people find hardest. The surface flakes, sometimes in pieces carrying visible colour, and it itches.

  • Don't pick. Flakes come away on their own; pulling one that isn't ready is the most common cause of a patchy result.
  • Don't scratch. Tapping gently through clothing takes the edge off the urge without touching the surface.
  • Keep it moisturised thinly. Dry skin itches more. Thick layers are not more effective, only more occlusive. A simple barrier ointment is all this step needs.
  • Coloured flakes are normal. Seeing pigment come away is alarming and is usually just surface material.

Stage three — the dull phase

Once the flaking finishes, a new layer of skin sits over the work and the tattoo looks cloudy, matte, or as though it has faded. Almost everybody worries at this point, and almost nobody needs to. It is a layer of skin, and it thins.

This is also the stage where people go back to the studio convinced something has gone wrong. Give it time before you do — though if you want reassurance, your artist would far rather send a two-line message than have you fretting for a fortnight.

Stage four — settling

The surface clears and the definition comes back. Colours read properly again. The skin looks like skin. On the surface this is generally a matter of weeks; the deeper layers continue for longer, which is why artists usually ask you to wait before booking a touch-up.

Long-term

  • Sun is the main factor in how a tattoo looks over years. Once the skin has fully settled, sunscreen on the area is the single most useful habit.
  • Keep the skin moisturised as ordinary routine.
  • Touch-ups are common and often expected — ask your artist when they want to reassess, rather than booking early.

What is not ordinary at any stage

Spreading redness, a red streak moving away from the area, increasing rather than easing pain, significant swelling, discharge that is not clear plasma, or a fever. Any of those is a reason to contact a pharmacist, your GP or NHS 111 promptly. A guide cannot assess your skin and this one is not trying to.

faq.question: How long does a tattoo take to heal?
faq.answer: The surface generally settles over a matter of weeks, and the deeper layers continue for longer — which is why artists usually ask you to wait before booking a touch-up. Placement, size, your skin and your artist's method all move the timeline.

faq.question: Why does my tattoo look faded and cloudy?
faq.answer: That is the stage after flaking, when a new layer of skin sits over the work. It is extremely common, it worries almost everybody, and it thins. Give it time before assuming something has gone wrong.

faq.question: Is it normal for coloured flakes to come off?
faq.answer: Yes. Seeing pigment in the flakes is alarming and is usually just surface material. What causes patchy results is pulling flakes that aren't ready to come away.

faq.question: How do I deal with the itching?
faq.answer: Keep the skin moisturised thinly — dry skin itches more — and tap gently through clothing rather than scratching. Don't pick.

faq.question: When should I worry?
faq.answer: Spreading redness, a red streak moving away from the area, pain that increases rather than eases after the first days, significant swelling, discharge that is not clear plasma, or a fever. Contact a pharmacist, your GP or NHS 111 promptly rather than waiting it out.

faq.question: When can I book a touch-up?
faq.answer: Ask your artist when they want to reassess. Booking early is common and usually too early — the deeper layers are still settling after the surface looks finished.
